claims.text: Changes in superconducting transition temperature in these HEA superconductors are primarily governed by electronic-doping-induced variations in the density of states at the Fermi level rather than by chemical disorder or electron scattering.
(TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x thin films are superconducting over multiple mixing ratios.
Compared compositions of (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x can have comparable atomic-disorder levels despite having substantially different elemental compositions.
Electronic doping changes the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level mediates superconductivity by changing the electron–phonon coupling strength.
A higher density of states at the Fermi level enhances the pairing interaction and raises Tc within a BCS mechanism.
A lower density of states at the Fermi level suppresses Tc.
The Tc variation is independent of disorder when disorder remains comparable across the samples.
Increasing electron doping necessarily produces a higher density of states at the Fermi level in the proposed composition series.
Samples with increased electron doping and higher N(EF) will have a higher Tc than the baseline despite comparable chemical disorder.
(TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x at x approximately 0.35 has Tc of about 6.7 K.
The compared x = 0.35 and x = 0.71 films have mean free paths of approximately 5–6 nm.
The compared x = 0.35 and x = 0.71 films have almost equivalent mixing entropy.
Comparable mean free path and mixing entropy can be used to establish comparable microscopic disorder in these films.
A critical level of disorder can suppress superconductivity near the Anderson quantum phase transition.
Multiband or unconventional superconducting effects may invalidate the proposed BCS density-of-states mechanism.
Existing evidence establishes a correlation among electron doping, density-of-states changes, and Tc variation in this alloy system.
The quantitative contributions of electronic doping and residual disorder vary with the specific alloy system.
